questions.stem: What is Information Modelling concerned with?
options: How information is described, structured and communicated so it is clearly understood and consistently interpreted
How servers are provisioned for applications
How reports are formatted for printing
questions.explanation: Information Modelling is the discipline of describing, structuring and communicating information so that people, processes and systems interpret it consistently.

questions.stem: What is the primary goal of Information Modelling?
questions.explanation: The primary goal is semantic clarity so information can be exchanged reliably across departments, systems and organisations.

questions.stem: Which statement about Information Modelling as a discipline is correct?
options: It is a single modelling technique
It is another name for BPMN
It is a family of approaches sharing the goal of representing business facts accurately and consistently
It only applies to unstructured data
questions.explanation: Information Modelling is not a single technique but a family of approaches, including NIAM, ORM and FCO-IM, that share a common goal.

questions.stem: Which three techniques are named as falling under the Information Modelling discipline?
questions.explanation: NIAM, ORM and FCO-IM are the named techniques that provide structured ways to verbalise facts and transform them into conceptual or logical models.

questions.stem: Which question does Information Modelling ask instead of how data will be stored?
options: What facts exist in the business, how they are expressed in language and how they relate
questions.explanation: Information Modelling emphasises meaning over implementation, asking what facts exist, how they are expressed and how they relate.

questions.stem: What was the limitation of early, natural-language-based fact modelling approaches?
options: They were too formal to read
They could not be read by business users
They only worked for numeric data
They were intuitive and business-friendly but limited in rigour and precision
questions.explanation: Early approaches focused on natural language, making models easy to understand but sometimes lacking precision.

questions.stem: What was the trade-off introduced by the more formal second stage of Information Modelling approaches?
options: Improved accuracy through constraints and structure, sometimes at the cost of readability
Improved readability at the cost of accuracy
Lower cost at the expense of tooling
questions.explanation: Later approaches introduced more formal structures and constraints to improve accuracy, though sometimes at the cost of readability.

questions.stem: What is the focus of the most recent evolution of Information Modelling?
options: How facts are communicated, preserving every nuance of business language for transformation into multiple technical representations
questions.explanation: Modern approaches model communication itself, ensuring nuances of business language are preserved and transformable into many technical outputs.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT listed as an output that modern information models can be transformed into?
questions.explanation: Named outputs are ER diagrams, UML models, XML schemas, semantic web representations and even executable systems; spreadsheet macros are not mentioned.

questions.stem: What key insight does the evolution of Information Modelling reflect?
options: Information is only stored, never communicated
Information is not just stored, it is communicated; how a fact is spoken or interpreted matters as much as how it is implemented
Diagrams are always better than sentences
Databases should be designed before facts are understood
Business users should not validate models
questions.explanation: The key insight is that information is communicated, not just stored, so how a fact is expressed matters as much as its later implementation.
